bib.title: The Survey of Retrieval-Augmented Text Generation in Large Language Models

question: How can the retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) literature be organised into a unified framework from an information retrieval viewpoint, and how is it evaluated?
contributions: A unified RAG paradigm split into pre-retrieval, retrieval, post-retrieval and generation phases (Sec 2)
A taxonomy of core techniques with representative studies (Fig 3) and a per-study summary of retrieval source, multi-hop, training and phase coverage (Table 2) and retrievers/generators (Table 3)
Pseudo-code for iterative, recursive, conditional and adaptive retrieval strategies (Algorithms 1-4)
An overview of RAG evaluation frameworks (Table 1) and a discussion of challenges and future directions

results.claim: On the MIRAGE medical QA benchmark, GPT-3.5 with no retrieval (CoT) averages 60.69 accuracy; adding PubMed with the domain retriever MedCPT raises it to 69.38.
results.setup: GPT-3.5 on MIRAGE (MMLU-Med, MedQA-US, MedMCQA, PubMedQA*, BioASQ-Y/N), PubMed corpus 23.9M docs, MedCPT retriever, average over five datasets
results.table: Table 4, rows None and PubMed (23.9M) / MedCPT, column Average
results.note: Data sourced from Mirage [144]; the survey did not run it.

results.claim: The best average over PubMed is RRF-2 (70.26), and combining four retrievers (RRF-4) is not better than two on Wikipedia.
results.setup: GPT-3.5 on MIRAGE, PubMed corpus, Reciprocal Rank Fusion of two retrievers; Wikipedia corpus RRF-2 60.14 vs RRF-4 59.14
results.table: Table 4, row PubMed RRF-2, column Average; Wikipedia RRF-2 60.14, RRF-4 59.14

results.claim: PubMedQA* accuracy rises from 36.00 with no retrieval to 66.20 with BM25 over PubMed, while Wikipedia BM25 gives 26.40, so corpus match to the task dominates.
results.setup: GPT-3.5, PubMedQA* subset of MIRAGE, BM25
results.table: Table 4, row PubMed BM25, column PubMedQA*

results.claim: A domain-specific retriever matched to the corpus helps; a generic retriever excels only where its training data matches (Contriever on Wikipedia).
Retrieval quality moves RAG performance more than generator choice; LLaMA2-7B with retrieval beats LLaMA2-70B closed-book.
results.setup: BERGEN: closed book vs oracle passages averaged over KILT QA datasets, LLMeval metric; eRAG: NQ with BM25, RetroMAE, SPLADEv3, DeBERTa-v3 re-ranking

limits: A survey: it ran no experiments of its own; the only numbers are reported from MIRAGE [144], BERGEN [114] and eRAG [119].
Table 2 and Table 3 give no counts or effect sizes for the statements drawn from them (multi-hop preference, BM25 use).
The ACM reference block still has placeholder conference text and DOI; the paper is a preprint.
Coverage of indexing is shallow: graph, PQ and LSH get a paragraph each with no recall or latency numbers except AiSAQ. LSH is called rarely used in RAG without a citation.
Cutoff is early to mid 2024 (arXiv v2 Aug 2024); later work such as agentic and long-context RAG is absent.
practices: Choose the indexing granularity by task: sentence level for QA, document level for summarisation (Sec 2.2.1).
Use ANN indexes (graph/HNSW, PQ, LSH) for dense vectors because exact search over vast collections is too costly; this trades a slight accuracy loss for speed (Sec 3.1).
Match the retriever to the corpus: domain-trained retrievers on domain corpora, and do not assume more fused retrievers is better (Sec 8.2).
Apply a heavier re-ranker only to the limited candidate set retrieved, since accurate but slow models fit there (Sec 2.2.3).
Pick the retrieval strategy by need: basic for simplicity, iterative for multi-step, recursive for hierarchical data, conditional for rules, adaptive for dynamic scenarios (Sec 4.2).
Evaluate retrieval at document level with the LLM as consumer (eRAG) rather than only with human relevance labels (Sec 7.1).
Invest in better retrieval before larger generators (Sec 8.2).

terms.definition: This approach significantly speeds up the search process at the cost of a slight reduction in search accuracy.
It accelerates searches by segmenting vectors and then clustering each part for quantization.
The core idea of LSH is to place similar vectors into the same hash bucket with high probability.
This structure associates documents with words to form a vocabulary list, allowing users to quickly locate references where a specific word appears within a collection of documents.

dynamically adjusts the retrieval strategy based on the context and nature of the query or the data retrieved so far.
